items.title: A response the same person flagged UNACCEPTABLE is ranked FIRST by that person on that prompt
items.measurement: 2988 assessments veto SOME but not all responses; 5952 of their rankings had a first place to contradict; 263 put a vetoed response there (4.42%). Excluded as coherent rather than contradictory: 195 assessments vetoing all four (a least-bad ordering) and 24 fully tied rankings (no first place). Examples (block, ranking, vetoed): [('personal', 'B>C>D=A', ['B', 'D']), ('world', 'B>C>D=A', ['B', 'D']), ('world', 'A>C>B>D', ['A', 'D'])]
items.falsifier: zero rankings placing a self-vetoed response first

items.title: The veto and personal-ranking questions were asked only in each annotator's first batch, so those fields are not a sample of the corpus
items.measurement: assessments per annotator: [(2, 15), (3, 2), (4, 1), (5, 61), (6, 4), (7, 2)] ... max 39. Assessments WITH a veto block per annotator: [(2, 15), (3, 4), (4, 1), (5, 992)] ... max 5

items.title: Rationale reuse and very short rationales indicate low-effort responding
items.measurement: 1012 annotators wrote 18657 world rationales; 8 reuse the same text for at least two thirds of their prompts; 3045 rationales (16.3%) are under 20 characters
items.falsifier: no annotator reusing rationales and no rationale under 20 characters

items.title: The personal and world rankings are largely the same answer given twice
items.measurement: 5006 assessments carry both rankings; 2609 are byte-identical (52.1%) and 2397 differ. The card frames them as personal taste versus an impartial societal view.
items.falsifier: an identical-share below 70%

items.title: Response SLOT predicts first and last place at high significance, but a slot-only predictor scores 0.4993 against 0.5000 chance -- real and worth nothing
items.measurement: on the 16530 rankings with a UNIQUE first place (88.5% of 18678): {'A': 4215, 'B': 3664, 'C': 4268, 'D': 4383}, chi-square 74.4 on 3 df against 16.27 at p=.001. Slot B is -11.3% versus uniform. Unique LAST place is stronger still: {'A': 3207, 'B': 2901, 'C': 2863, 'D': 3914}, chi-square 220.7, with slot D +21.5%.
items.falsifier: a chi-square below 16.27 on the unique-first-place subset

items.title: Some responses do not end in terminal punctuation, the signature of a truncated generation
items.measurement: 42 of 4312 responses (1.0%) end without terminal punctuation
items.falsifier: a rate below 5%

items.title: Some compiled criteria are reused verbatim across different prompts, which is the signature of a generic criterion in a prompt-specific rubric
items.measurement: 3883 distinct core criteria, 13 appearing on more than one prompt; most reused: [('maintain a neutral, descriptive tone.', 4), ('keep the response concise.', 3), ('use plain, accessible language.', 2)]

items.measurement: 122667 within-prompt criterion pairs; 243 exceed 0.85 text similarity (0.20%). The compiler's stated job includes removing redundancy, so these are what it had to work with.
items.falsifier: zero pairs above 0.85 similarity

items.measurement: 14984 criteria; 1904 contain a non-ASCII character, of which 105 remain after removing curly quotes, en/em dashes, ellipses and bullets. Examples: ['Dismiss the user’s concerns with clichés like “just follow y', 'ejemplicar escenarios en caso de cada decisión y consecuenci']

items.measurement: 15248 criteria; 433 (2.8%) contain an explicitly evaluative word such as good, better, appropriate or helpful, which the quiz drilled as the marker of a SUBJECTIVE criterion; 100 (0.7%) open with a generic quality adjective rather than anything prompt-specific

items.measurement: mean response length by slot: {'A': 520, 'B': 519, 'C': 517, 'D': 513}; spread relative to the mean = 1.5%

items.title: CHECKED: no boilerplate opening or closing recurs across responses

items.title: WITHDRAWN: my harm regex matches harm WORDS inside criteria that prohibit them, so the 66.7% figure measures the regex and not the release
items.measurement: 1155 criteria mention a harm term such as misinformation, slur, violence or fabricate; 770 of them (66.7%) carry a positive mean weight, i.e. the aggregation rewards a response for doing it. Separately, 696 criteria OPEN with an explicit prohibition and 540 (77.6%) are positively weighted. Examples (weight, text): [(5.9, "use people‑first language like 'undocumented immigrant' instead of the term 'ill"), (4.0, 'Clarify terminology (e.g., "illegal" vs. "undocumented")'), (4.8, 'The model should describe any exclusionary tactics without resorting to sexist s')]
items.falsifier: harm-naming criteria being uniformly negatively weighted

items.title: CHECKED: no duplicate prompt texts
items.measurement: 1078 prompts, 0 exact-duplicate texts
items.falsifier: zero duplicate prompt texts

items.title: Very short criteria are unlikely to be checkable against a response
items.measurement: 38 of 15248 criteria (0.2%) are under 25 characters
items.falsifier: no criterion under 25 characters

items.title: CHECKED: the position effect is statistically real but worth essentially NOTHING on the metric everything here uses
items.measurement: a fixed score vector derived from corpus-wide first-place frequencies, applied identically to all 18678 rankings, reaches pairwise concordance 0.4993 against a chance level of 0.5000 -- a difference of -0.0007. Wave one measured the slot effect at chi-square 74.4 on first place and 220.7 on last, both far past p=.001. Both are true: at n=16,530 a tiny asymmetry is overwhelmingly significant AND carries no predictive power. Wave one called this BLOCKING; on this evidence that was wrong.
items.falsifier: a slot-only predictor departing from 0.5000 by more than 0.01

wrong_answers.empty list: Any analysis defaulting `.get(k, [])` counts 13,672 never-asked questions as answered-zero. Veto rates come out 82.9% instead of 36.4%; a concentration ratio comes out 5.01x instead of 2.56x. I made both errors.
wrong_answers.first batch: The veto and personal-ranking fields are capped at five per annotator, so any rate computed over the full corpus is diluted roughly fourfold, and any per-person statistic on them has n=5 at most.
wrong_answers.No authorship field: Treating the criterion pool as human normative input attributes 5,564 lab-written seeds to participants. Any claim about 'what people wrote' is 36% not what people wrote.
wrong_answers.no pointer to their source: Lineage from a compiled criterion back to its source can only be recovered by text matching, which succeeds for 7.8% verbatim and 30.8% at 0.80 similarity. Any claim that a criterion 'survived' compilation is a text-similarity guess.
wrong_answers.where the four candidate responses came: Nothing supports a claim about what generated the candidates, so any statement about model behaviour rather than about these 4,312 specific texts is unfounded.
wrong_answers.UNACCEPTABLE is ranked FIRST: Treating the veto as a hard constraint and the ranking as consistent with it will silently contradict itself on 4.4% of vetoing assessments.
wrong_answers.essentially every annotator: Any inter-annotator agreement statistic leans hardest on the one prompt everyone saw -- and that prompt's text is garbled, so the agreement estimate is anchored on a test artefact.
wrong_answers.no rubric at all: Joining rubrics to prompts silently drops 110 of 1,078 prompts, and they are not a random remainder: they average 25.4 assessments against 16.1.
wrong_answers.two files with different coverage: Reading assessments from comparisons.jsonl gives 293 fewer than reading them from annotators.jsonl. The two files are not interchangeable.
wrong_answers.disjoint id namespaces: There is no key to join rubrics to prompts. Any pipeline assuming one will silently produce an empty result, which reads as 'no data' rather than as 'wrong join'.
wrong_answers.Two different message schemas: A loader written for one file returns empty text for the other. Mine did, for 1,095 of 1,095 prompts, and every downstream feature came out constant without an error.
wrong_answers.near-binary: Treating the -10..+10 scale as interval-valued over-weights the endpoints, which carry 17% of all ratings.
wrong_answers.concentrated in a few countries: Any 'collective' or 'crowd' aggregate is an aggregate over a panel that is 63% three countries.
wrong_answers.attributable to a single annotator: 9,684 free-text criteria are linkable to one person each, alongside their age, gender, country and education.
wrong_answers.synthetic and short: Median user turn is 139 characters and the card calls the prompts synthetic, so nothing here transfers to production traffic.
wrong_answers.leaked into the prompt text: Eight prompts carry generation scaffolding or pretext framing. An annotator answering one is doing a different task, and nothing marks which.
wrong_answers.name a response as best: Rationale text and ranking disagree in 12.6% of cases where someone states plainly which response is best, so the two cannot both be used as ground truth.
wrong_answers.same answer given twice: Personal and world rankings are byte-identical in 52.1% of assessments carrying both, so treating them as two independent judgements double-counts one.
wrong_answers.identical ranking string: Six annotators with five or more prompts submit the same ranking every time, and nothing flags them.
wrong_answers.SLOT predicts: Statistically real and worth nothing: a slot-only predictor scores 0.4993 against 0.5000 chance. Do not correct for it and do not cite it as a defect with consequences.
